articleTitle: CBSE ‘hack’, IIT gig and US recognition: Nisarga Adhikary’s incredible year at 19
articleFeaturedImageAlt: nisarga
description: The cybersecurity researcher, who is now working at IIT Kanpur, was recognised by the US Department of Justice for reporting a vulnerability in one of its systems
body_raw: Tuesday, September 22. It was almost an hour past midnight. Nisarga Adhikary was sitting in the Starbucks caf at IIT Kanpur. An email notification flashed across his screen. It was a message from the US Department of Justice, acknowledging his work in finding and reporting a security flaw within their systems. I was having my second cup of coffee when I received the email, he recalls. Nisarga Adhikary is only 19 years old. On paper, this recognition stood as one of the most prestigious accolades he could have ever imagined. Yet, surprisingly, he remained unfazed, showing no trace of excitement. I love to break stuff, Nisarga says. Hacking things is a part of me trying to understand how things work. The security flaw was not something he had been assigned to find. There was no college project or professional brief behind it. He was simply trying to understand how the system worked. Still, the recognition was the latest turn in a remarkable five months for this 19-year-old. In February, he first drew public attention for identifying alleged security flaws in the Central Board of Secondary Educations digital examination system and has since landed a job at IIT Kanpurs cybersecurity hub. Nisarga is from Siliguri, West Bengal. His parents, both senior government officers, wanted him to take the Joint Entrance Examination JEE and he was preparing through a FIITJEE South Delhi programme. Then, his work began attracting attention. His parents were worried, Nisarga says, before they gradually became more accepting of it. The CBSE controversy Earlier this year, Nisarga began examining publicly accessible parts of CBSEs On-Screen Marking OSM system, the digital platform used to evaluate scanned answer sheets. He claims he found several weaknesses in the system. One, its One-Time Password OTP checks could be bypassed, allowing an unauthorised user to access examiner accounts without receiving an actual code. Two, poorly configured storage on Amazon Web Services AWS allegedly gave him access to about 1.8 million scanned answer sheets. Nisarga also demonstrated the account-takeover risk by accessing the account of a physics teacher on the live CBSE system. Asked about the ethics of accessing a real persons account, he says hed blurred the teachers details and used the access only to demonstrate the vulnerability. He reported his findings to the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team CERT-In, the government agency that coordinates responses to cybersecurity incidents, in February. By May, he had published a detailed account of what he had found. He had also come on television to describe and explain his findings. His revelations quickly attracted attention as students, teachers, and parents were already raising concerns about glitches, evaluation inconsistencies, and operational problems linked to the OSM rollout. The board initially denied that its OSM portal had been compromised, but later acknowledged that cybersecurity issues had been flagged in the public domain. Subsequently, on May 31, CBSE stated that it had been closely monitoring the vulnerabilities in the OnMark portal and that a team of cybersecurity professionals drawn from various arms of the government as well as the IITs had been deployed over the last few days to fortify the system. Nisargas findings soon became part of a wider political debate. Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi was among those who publicly praised him for raising questions about the CBSE system. Nisarga also participated in protests organised by the Cockroach Janta Party CJP over the NEET-UG paper leak and posted a photograph with CJP convenor Abhijeet Dipke. He says he was invited to meet Rahul Gandhi alongside Sarthak Sidhant, who had separately flagged alleged irregularities in CBSEs tendering process, but chose not to go. Sarthak, an 18-year-old student from Jharkhand, had known Nisarga before they became publicly associated with the CBSE controversy. He says they met around three years ago on Reddit and credits Nisarga with supporting him during CBSE times. Kshitij Kapoor, a software engineer at AI research lab Nous Research, says he has known Nisarga since he was 14. He met him through Capture The Flag CTF, competitive cybersecurity exercises where players find hidden text strings called flags inside vulnerable systems or programmes. Hes always had a knack for poking holes in systems. The curiosity hasnt changed much but the scale definitely has, Kshitij says. I was happy to see him get recognition. Having known him since so early on, it felt very personal to me in a way. The teen behind the screen Nisarga describes himself as a nerd all his life. He says he spends almost all his waking hours glued to a screen, claiming that he has no non-technical friends. Outside cybersecurity, he reads young-adult fiction, like The Fault in Our Stars. He is also a big fan of Japanese animation such as Tokyo Ghoul. He reads books about activism and says he is interested in activism for the rights of neurodivergent people, queer rights and internet freedom. His views on technology and society are shaped, he says, by what he calls neoliberal technocratic biases. He describes himself as socially very left and economically right. He looks up to the likes of Sam Altman and Mark Zuckerberg, the heads of the artificial intelligence company OpenAI and technology company Meta, respectively, for their drive to build things. From exam-system sleuth to IIT Kanpur Around the same time, Nisargas views on technology and government brought him to the attention of IIT Kanpur Director Manindra Agrawal. When the Centre moved to restrict Telegram before the NEET-UG re-exam, Nisarga criticised the decision, arguing that authorities had failed to prevent paper leaks while trying to restrict a messaging platform that could still be accessed through proxies. IIT Kanpur director Manindra Agrawal responded to his comments, saying he would need to sit Nisarga down and explain. He had already reached out to the teenager earlier, and the interaction eventually led to Nisarga joining C3iHub, IIT Kanpurs cybersecurity-focused technology innovation hub, as an Open-Source Intelligence OSINT and Threat Intelligence Engineer. His job involves identifying and understanding potential security threats. Nisarga, however, remains sceptical of an educational system that measures people through examinations and credentials alone. You can have a PhD and still produce low quality research and do worse than your peers with no degree. It depends on talent and curiosity, he says. For now, he is settling into life at IIT Kanpur. He says the transition has not been difficult, although he describes Kanpur as a bit bad compared with places he has lived before. Eventually, he wants to work across technology, defence and artificial intelligence and may eventually return to formal education, possibly in the US or another country. For someone whose curiosity began with figuring out how computer systems work, the question now is what he will choose to explore next. But when that email from the US Department of Justice arrived, Nisarga did not see it as a defining moment for him. I was unamused. It was like any other normal Hall of Fame mention for me, he says. I think I work a lot and put all my time into research because thats the only coping mechanism I have. Why is he unmoved by this latest recognition? Alex Karp, CEO of Palantir once said that one cannot have a great social life at age 20 and achieve extraordinary career success at the same time, he says. It might sound toxic but hes kind of right, I feel.

articleTitle: Nearly 200 isolated after lab worker dies of suspected plague in Siberia
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Russia-plague case
description: A lab worker at an anti-plague institute in Siberia has died, and nearly 200 people are under medical watch. Russia has not confirmed plague.
body_raw: Russian authorities have quarantined medical facilities in Siberia and put nearly 200 people under medical observation after the death of a woman who worked at an anti-plague laboratory. Russian media have said she may have had pneumonic plague, but health authorities have not yet confirmed the illness, according to Axios. The woman is named as Daria Shipilova, 28, a laboratory assistant at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. Local reports say she broke a test tube holding the bacteria. Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev said none of the people being watched has shown symptoms, and all their tests so far have come back negative. A Trump administration official told Axios on Sunday that the White House is monitoring the case. Russias public health agency says the situation in the region is stable. In a thread on X, health expert Ashish K. Jha said he is concerned and that Russia owes the world more answers. Not all of these claims have been checked, and the cause of the death has not been confirmed by officials. Many of you have been tracking the Irkutsk lab situation over the last few days. Ive been gathering facts and trying to understand what is happening before weighing in. Now that I have, I have to say - Im concerned - Ashish K. Jha ashishkjha October 5, 2026 What happened to the lab worker Local reports say Shipilova broke a test tube containing the pneumonic plague pathogen on September 25. Later, she fell ill on an expedition with other workers near Russias eastern border with Mongolia, The New York Post reported, citing the news outlet Lyudi Baikala. She was admitted to a hospital in the town of Shelekhov on September 29 with signs of severe pneumonia. According to reports in the Post and Axios, Shipilova was placed on a ventilator and died in the intervening night between October 1 and 2 After her death, authorities put quarantines in place at several medical facilities in the region. Workers in protective gear have been testing people and places in Shelekhov, the Post said. What is plague Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. It killed tens of millions of people in the Black Death in the Middle Ages, the Post said. There are three main forms bubonic, pneumonic and septicemic. Symptoms can include fever, headache, chills, weakness, shortness of breath and cough. All forms can be treated with antibiotics, especially when treatment starts early, according to the Post and the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, as cited by Axios. Claims of a cover-up The Post said the case has led to accusations that Russian authorities are trying to keep details out of public view. The Russian political channel Nezygar said the situation in Shelekhov resembles the Wuhan case. Mikhal Favorov, a senior Russian epidemiologist, disputed the broken test tube account, The Moscow Times reported. He said staff at an anti-plague institute wear protective suits, so the risk of infection from a broken tube is very low. He said the story was one the public would accept, and that Popovas trip suggested the situation was serious. He also said people would not be told what really happened. These are the views of one expert and one Telegram channel. No evidence of a cover-up was given in the sources. White House response A Trump administration official told Axios the administration is aware, monitoring the outbreak, and assessing options. White House spokespeople sent questions to the State Department, which did not reply to a request for comment, Axios said. Ashish K. Jha, a health expert, posted a thread on X on Sunday about the Irkutsk case. He said he had spent days gathering facts before commenting and that he is now concerned. He summed up what is known a 28-year-old technician at an anti-plague institute reportedly broke a tube holding the plague pathogen on 25 September, she died on 1 or 2 October, and nearly 200 people are in medical isolation. Heres what we know. A 28-year-old technician at an anti-plague institute reportedly broke a tube containing plague pathogen on September 25. She died October 1 or 2. Nearly 200 people are now in medical isolation 2n- Ashish K. Jha ashishkjha October 5, 2026 What Russian officials have said Anna Popova, who heads Russias public-health watchdog, travelled about 2,600 miles from Moscow to the Irkutsk region, the Post said. She has not commented in public. Kobzev did not name the illness and called it a dangerous infection. He cancelled all public events in the region and asked people to stay calm after meeting Popova. On Telegram on Friday, he said all identified contacts are under medical observation, show no signs of illness and have tested negative. Russias public health agency said Shipilova had pneumonia of unknown cause, according to Axios. It said further tests found no microorganisms linked to her work and that the epidemiological situation in the region remains stable. The Post also cited reports that antibiotics had run out in the Irkutsk region, which led worried residents to seek help at pharmacies and other medical facilities. This has not been confirmed by officials.

articleTitle: ‘I want to feel safe’: Young women attempt to march towards Jantar Mantar
articleFeaturedImageAlt: jantar mantar protest, gyanesh kumar
description: Meanwhile, many independent journalists and other protesters, who had sat outside the Parliament Street police station till Saturday night demanding accountability, returned on Sunday morning to demand the registration of an FIR into the allegations raised by the three women journalists.
body_raw: As the march from Andhra Bhavan Canteen towards Jantar Mantar reached Ashoka Road on Sunday, Adira 26 stood on the side of the road in silence, clutching her friends hand as she watched the crowd. The final-year law student, originally from Kerala and studying at Delhi University, had initially not planned to join the protest, which has been underway since October 2 demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner CEC Gyanesh Kumar. However, Sundays march was not focused solely on alleged irregularities in the Election Commission of India. It also voiced concerns over womens safety, coming a day after three women journalists accused Delhi Police officers of alleged sexual harassment while covering the stir near Jantar Mantar. Womens safety in the Capital has dominated conversations since the alleged gangrape of a minor girl by three men posing as police officers at a park in Delhi last month. Against this backdrop of rising crimes against women in the Capital, Adira said she felt compelled to join the march. I want to feel safe, she said. I came to Delhi in 2023, and when I was staying in a hostel, there were several restrictions. I wasnt allowed to wear sleeveless tops in our own premises, she said. Her parents were hesitant to send her to the Capital and have grown more worried since the news of the gangrape of the minor at a park in September. They called and told me to discontinue the course and come back, but how can I?, she said. Standing beside Adira was her friend Ayushi 20, also a DU student, from Champawat, Uttarakhand. For Ayushi, the fight has been long and is often unfair. Even in 2026, we have to fight for our basic rights. Crime happens against women but eventually they are the only one that suffers., she said, recalling how classes at DUs Lady Shri Ram College had moved online after the alleged gangrape last month. Already we have very little freedom, dont go here, dont wear such clothes. Even after any crime happens, were the ones that get blamed, she said. Another protester, Saniya Ali 18, said she had lied to her parents, who are based in Bihar, to join the protest in the Capital, telling them she was going to Delhi only for exploring. Today Im here because I think I need to. I stayed here because I have many questions to ask Prime Minister Narendra Modi. I want to ask him, what all is not happening here. Votes are being stolen, women are being raped, what is our country doing? Yesterday I was detained, were here to ask for justice. They are scared that were again seeking resignation. I lied because my parents will be scared if I go out and something happens, but I do not blame them completely, she said. Meanwhile, many independent journalists and other protesters, who had sat outside the Parliament Street police station till Saturday night demanding accountability, returned on Sunday morning to demand the registration of an FIR into the allegations raised by the three women journalists. The Crime Branch has now been tasked with investigating the matter, officers said on Saturday. Rishabh Ranjan, who works with the All India Congress Committee AICC law department and represents one of the women journalists who raised the allegation against the officers, said the police still had not registered an FIR, even though she was taken to RML hospital last night for a Medico-Legal Case MLC. We had gone inside with an expectation that a senior police officer at least of a rank of DCP would speak to us and share what was the reason that they transferred the case to the Crime Branch. We dont know whether they have named the person in the complaint registered or not. We wanted them to register a zero FIR, he said.

articleTitle: Who is Alexis Wilkins, country singer engaged to FBI Director Kash Patel
articleFeaturedImageAlt: UFC Freedom 250 Trump
description: FBI Director Kash Patel and country singer Alexis Wilkins have announced their engagement. The couple has been dating since before Patel became FBI director in 2025.
body_raw: FBI Director Kash Patel got engaged to his longtime girlfriend, country singer Alexis Wilkins. The couple announced their engagement in a post on X on Sunday evening. Alexis Wilkins, 27, shared a black-and-white photo of herself with Kash Patel, 46, showing her engagement ring. She captioned the post Went and got the law involved. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Alexis Wilkins alexiswilkins Kash Patel and Alexis Wilkins have been dating since before he became FBI director in 2025, when she attended his swearing-in ceremony. Who is Alexis Wilkins? Alexis Wilkins met Kash Patel in late 2022 at a party hosted by country musician John Rich in Nashville. Patel, then a Truth Social consultant and former Trump aide, was selling KH merchandise and books praising Donald Trump. Wilkins, who was trying to launch her country music career, was introduced to him at the party. They began dating by early 2023. Wilkins grew up partly in London and Switzerland and attended elementary school in Geneva before graduating from Belmont University in Nashville in 2020. She briefly pursued acting in Los Angeles, appearing in two episodes of Modern Family, before focusing on country music. Her debut single, Holdin On, was released in 2020. She now performs patriotic songs at conservative events, though her website lists no upcoming shows. Country music critic Kyle Coroneos described her as an aspiring artist and rated her rendition of the US national anthem 7.5 out of 10. Alexis Wilkins released her debut album in 2023 and has been affiliated with conservative groups. On her website, she describes her music as honouring country tradition while adding contemporary commentary. Wilkins also made headlines as a performer at President Donald Trumps Great American State Fair on the National Mall as part of America 250, as other artists pulled out of the event after finding out it was not a non-partisan celebration. FBI protective team escorted Alexis Wilkins to run errands, hair appointments According to a report by The New York Times, last April, FBI agents in two SUVs stood guard outside a senior centre in Dixon, Illinois, while Alexis Wilkins performed for a few dozen young conservatives. Dianna Muller, founder of Women for Gun Rights, which briefly employed Wilkins as a spokeswoman, said When Kash got confirmed, life changed for her. Kash Patel has faced criticism over his use of government aircraft for trips with no known or apparent law enforcement purpose. This included an FBI jet flight to State College, Pennsylvania, for a pro-wrestling event where Alexis Wilkins performed the national anthem. Alexis Wilkins also had a full-time protective team comprising Special Weapons and Tactics team members from FBI field offices across the US, The New York Times reported. The team accompanied her to engagements including singing appearances and even a hair appointment. In May 2025, Kash Patel attended a secret national security conference at an exclusive resort outside London and invited Alexis Wilkins to a group dinner with King Charles III at Windsor Castle. When UK police declined to pick her up from the airport, the FBI arranged tactical agents and an embassy vehicle for her, according to a report by The New York Times. The disclosure raised questions over the use of taxpayer-funded resources for Patels personal activities. An FBI spokesman told the New York Times that active death threats against Wilkins warranted the level of protection she was receiving.

articleTitle: Janhvi Kapoor calls her Chuttamalle AI video with NTR ‘assault’: ‘Reality of being a woman’
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Janhvi Kapoor opens up on AI edits of her Devara song "Chuttamalle".
description: Jr NTR and Janhvi Kapoor were featured in deepfake video of the Chuttamalle song. The actress has finally reacted to the ongoing controversy.
body_raw: Actor Janhvi Kapoor has called out the misuse of AI to objectify women as an AI-generated inappropriate video featuring her with Devara co-star Jr NTR from the track Chuttamalle emerged on social media. She compared the explicit video to assault as many leading voices from the South film industries supported her. The morphed clip showed Janhvi in a sexually explicit scene, that was never a part of the original song. After the video went viral on the internet, NTR criticised such distasteful videos, threatening legal action against them. Chiranjeevi, Khushbu Sundar, Vijay Deverakonda, and others also extended their support to Janhvi. Taking to her Instagram handle, Janhvi Kapoor slammed the criminal misuse of technology. The criminal misuse of technology to objectify women and circulate fictionalised content without consent is deeply violating, bordering on sexual assault. Almost every woman in my industry has faced some version of this, and women everywhere are increasingly being subjected to it, she started her long note. ALSO READ Janhvi Kapoor lauds Telugu film industrys work hours Nap for 20 minutes The actor continued, Consent, choice and respect for a womans body should be among the most basic notions of humanity. Yet somehow, they continue to be treated as complicated. They are not. It is surprising that it still seems too nuanced for some people to understand that even if a woman says yes five days in a row and no on the sixth, that no must be respected. If she happens to wear a miniskirt, it does not give anyone permission to put a camera up her skirt, capture violating angles or visually exploit her body. What a woman is comfortable with, where she draws the line and what she chooses to do with her body are decisions that belong exclusively to her. This is basic. Janhvi mentioned that the issue goes beyond what she has ever experienced in her entire career. It is about the larger reality of being a woman, the gaze, the judgement, the constant negotiation for safety, and the feeling that our boundaries somehow remain open to interpretation. That threat has now expanded into the digital sphere, when we have not even adequately addressed the very real, physical fear that continues to disrupt the lives of women every day. She highlighted that facing such things is a reality of being a woman. To conclude her note, she thanked her co-star NTR, and other actors for their support, including, Chiranjeevi, Vijay Deverakonda and Khushbu Sundar. I am deeply touched by NTR sir for taking such a strong stand and condemning this violation. Thank you, sir. When someone whom millions look up to speaks up about something that may not directly concern him, it makes a difference to every woman who has experienced some degree of this behaviour. Thank you also to Chiranjeevi sir, Vijay and Khushbu maam for amplifying that sentiment and calling for action against this mentality and these immoral practices. Janhvi Kapoor and Jr NTRs film Devara Part 1 released in September 2024. The concerned song Chuttamalle, was composed by Anirudh Ravichander and sung by Shilpa Rao, turning out to be one of the most famous tracks from the film.

articleTitle: OpenAI’s Sam Altman says AI benefits warrant accepting some risks
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Sam Altman said that OpenAI has signed a deal with the US government to deploy AI models in the Department of War's classified networks.
description: Altman said there remained a fundamental difference in worldview between OpenAI and rival Anthropic on AI ⁠regulation.
body_raw: OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman said the benefits of artificial intelligence justify accepting some risks and argued the technology should remain broadly accessible to the public We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency, Altman said in an interview with Politicos technology-focused newsletter Decoded. Altman said there remained a fundamental difference in worldview between OpenAI and rival Anthropic on AI regulation, adding I think theres a lot of daylight. I disagree, but I understand the perspective of people who are like, This technology is going to get so powerful, and its so dangerous, that a single lab in San Francisco should have it and make sure nothing bad happens, and kind of figure out how to dole out the benefits, Altman said. He called that a completely unacceptable trade-off that runs counter to the lighter-touch regulatory stance backed by OpenAI. I wouldnt take a trade of saying, Well make sure theres no major hacks, theres no misuse of this technology, theres zero scams, theres zero all the other bad things that will happen, Altman said. Because I think people will do tremendously - orders of magnitude more - good stuff than bad stuff. Altmans remarks come amid a growing debate within the AI industry over the pace of development and the risks posed by increasingly capable systems. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in September published an essay calling on the industry to slow down to pace the frontier, a stance that Altman publicly endorsed. Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned in September, saying the people building AI believe it could kill us all by the end of the decade. Reuters reported in September that Anthropic warned that, despite AIs potential benefits, the technology can sometimes act in ways that run counter to its makers intentions and penetrate other companies systems. The company said advanced models could exhibit self-preserving behaviors, including attempts to resist shutdown, conceal or manipulate information, or generate outputs that could be interpreted as coercive, deceptive, or manipulative. However, US President Donald Trump has largely dismissed calls for new restrictions, arguing they would make it harder for American companies to compete with Chinese rivals. He has repeatedly said existing law enforcement agencies, including the Justice Department, provide sufficient safeguards and that no new rules are needed.

articleTitle: New process helps remove toxins, pick rare earth metals from wastewater
articleFeaturedImageAlt: IIT Gandhinagar engineers a 'Molecular Fishing Net' that filters toxic heavy metals and recovers rare earth elements from waste water. (Image credit: IIT Gandhinagar)
description: IIT Gandhinagar, University of Cambridge, and University of Birmingham researchers develop a method to remove toxic heavy metals from waste water and recover rare-earth elements in it
body_raw: Researchers from the Indian Institute of Technology, Gandhinagar IITGN, University of Cambridge and University of Birmingham have jointly developed a method that they said will help capture toxic metals and recover valuable rare earth elements RREs from waste water. The protocol uses highly porous materials called metal-organic frameworks MOFs, according to a study, published in Nature Protocols. We generally throw away a broken camera lens, earphones, or an old phone that has stopped working and is beyond repair. However, these objects have rare earth elements RREs that have applications in magnets, superconductivity, optics, and batteries, among others. When such objects become part of water, recovering REEs becomes difficult, said Superb Misra, Jibaben Patel Chair Professor in the Department of Materials Engineering, IITGN, and the Principal Investigator of the Bio Nano Materials Group. On the other hand, industrial activities can introduce toxic metals such as lead, cadmium, nickel and manganese into water, he said, adding that the challenge is removing these unwanted and harmful metal pollutants from water and recapturing the valuable REEs. How the filter works Researchers said the MOF functions as a molecular fishing net. Its countless pores spread out a vast catching surface, while specially designed chemical sites act like hooks that can latch on to particular metals. The researchers tuned this net in such a way that it preferentially traps the metals they are looking for. Simply speaking, it is like identifying and specifically picking red and green coloured marbles from a bucket containing hundreds of marbles in different colours, they explained. Some MOFs can have internal surface areas of up to 7,000 square metres per gram. To put that number in perspective, one gram may look like a tiny pinch of powder, but inside it is a surface area comparable to an entire football field. This huge internal surface makes MOFs very good adsorbents, they said. While conventional methods such as precipitation, coagulation and flocculation can be useful for water treatment, they are generally sensitive to pH, with optimal removal confined to narrow ranges. Broadly speaking, precipitation lets heavy impurities settle out, coagulation makes impurities clump together, and flocculation makes small impurity clumps collide and grow into larger clusters that can be separated, Prof Misra explained. Beyond laboratory Industrial effluents-discharged from manufacturing, mining, and chemical processing - entering water bodies contain several metals and contaminants such as pesticides, detergents and organic pollutants. The specially designed MOFs can be used as an adsorbent for the recovery and removal of metals under controlled conditions. The protocol was tested in complex real-world scenarios. For example, it was tested using wastewater that is alkaline pH over 8.5, turbid, and high in dissolved solid impurities. The method was also tested in artificial seawater and e-waste-derived samples. The workflow developed in this study can be applied to similar adsorbents and other contaminants, researchers said. The MOF, in our protocol, demonstrated substantial adsorption capacities, said Dhruv Menon, who did BTech from IITGN and is currently a doctoral student in the Department of Chemical Engineering and Biotechnology at the University of Cambridge, United Kingdom. One gram of copper-based MOF can capture nearly half a gram of lead 490 mgg, and roughly a quarter of a gram each of cadmium 264 mgg and manganese 226 mgg. For rare-earth elements, it could capture around one-third of a gram per gram of material 351 mgg of neodymium, 343 mgg of yttrium, 335 mgg of dysprosium, 337 mgg of terbium and 345 mgg of europium, Menon said, citing their experiments. Towards sustainability There is a need for approaches that can solve multiple environmental challenges simultaneously. Our focus was on engineering the performance of MOFs to employ them for environmental remediation applications. That said, it is crucial to understand that controlled batch experiments cannot fully predict behaviours in complex wastewater. There is a need to look at factors like large-scale fabrication, cost analyses, MOF life-cycle assessment and regulatory testing, Dr Misra said. Other team members involved in the study include Prathmesh Bhadane PhD, IITGN Postdoctoral fellow, IIT Bombay, Priya Mahato doctoral student, IITGN, Prateek Goyal PhD, IITGN, Dr Iseult Lynch Professor, School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Birmingham, UK, and Dr Swaroop Chakraborty NERC Fellow, University of Birmingham.

articleTitle: Asian Games tour diary: Earthquake warnings, getting lost underground and a city too polite to say ‘no’
articleFeaturedImageAlt: For much of the fortnight, I have had the feeling that Aichi-Nagoya does not really want to host the Asian Games, but is far too polite to say no. (PTI Photo)
description: Earthquake warnings, a station maze, a last cookie and a closing-ceremony horse from a fortnight in Aichi-Nagoya
body_raw: Day 0 Care, caution I land in Nagoya, pick up my credentials and receive a media kit. I think of the Tokyo Olympics, my last trip to Japan. The welcome kit for those pandemic Games came with dozens of tubes, bottles and QR codes, all tied to the daily ritual of Covid-19 testing. This time, there is no reminder to spit into those tubes before even brushing. Instead, there is earthquake and tsunami safety guidance. Navigating earthquakes, it turns out, is one of the trickier parts of living here. Around 1,500 earthquakes are felt across the country each year, most of them harmless. But the government warns of a magnitude 8-9 Nankai Trough earthquake in the next 30 years, and Nagoya, sitting in the Nankai region, is among the areas considered particularly vulnerable. Click here to read our Asian Games full coverage So, the warnings are everywhere. Evacuation zones are marked outside the athletes plaza. Safety advisories sit inside railway stations. Competition venues have their own instructions. Before play begins, the giant screen invariably flashes a reminder of what to do, and what not to do, in the event of an earthquake or tsunami. On the first day, I notice every one of them. Twenty-four hours later, I barely register them. The media kit contains another, more thoughtful item masks for neck, shoulder and leg pain. Because the other hazard of these Games is much less dramatic the walking. As the days pass, the step count keeps climbing. It peaks on October 1, when I travel between Nagoya, Obu and Okazaki, using the train-bus-train combination that has become something of a recurring feature of these Games. By the end of the day, I have covered 15.02 km on foot. If nothing else, these Games are going to do wonders for my annual step-count target. Day 1 Lost in the maze Nagoya Station is the sort of place that makes me question my own sense of direction. Above ground, there are trains, towers, roads and people moving in every direction. Below ground is another city platforms on different levels, underground passages disappearing around corners, shopping arcades, staircases, escalators and exits that seem to multiply the further I walk. While returning from a venue, I am completely lost. Google Maps suggests a train, then a bus to another station that would take me to Kinjofuto, where the main media hub is and the cruise liner for athletes is docked. I am used to the coarse pudhe chala move ahead of BEST conductors in Mumbai, the instruction delivered at full volume, with the assumption that I will somehow figure out the rest. Here, the woman bus driver wears a face mask, a crisp white shirt and a black jacket. At the Tokai-dori stop, she picks up the microphone and individually thanks every passenger who gets in. Arigato gozaimasu. There are perhaps 13-15 of us who get in. She thanks all of us. By the end of the day, at around 11.30pm, I am lost again somewhere underneath Nagoya. I am standing at a Kintetsu platform, staring at my phone and trying to work out whether the train waiting on Platform 1 will take me to Komeno, from where my apartment is a 7-minute walk. I find a uniformed woman and show her my phone. She squints at the screen. Nods. I hop in, and three minutes later, hop off. Then, just as the doors are about to close, the same woman steps out of the captains cabin. She looks at me. Checks that I have got off at the right station. Gives me a thumbs-up. Gets back in. The train chugs away into the darkness. I stand on the platform wondering if she really comes out just to make sure the lost foreigner gets off at the right station. Day 3 Early morning trek The city gradually disappears. The bus windows lose the towers and dense buildings. Then come fields, little houses, narrow roads, wooded slopes. By the time it drops us off, I am in a sleepy rural corner of Toyota City, with another kilometre to walk to the venue. It is early morning. The road is quiet. On either side are dense stands of trees, the hills rising behind them in layers of green. There are stretches where the only sound is my own footsteps. And somewhere inside this landscape is a shooting range. The venue is secluded, surrounded by the forest. It is a beautiful setting for a sport that demands a Zen-like state from its athletes. Reaching the venue and getting back takes up an entire day, but you dont really mind. By afternoon the weather changes, it starts to drizzle, then, almost theatrically, the sky turns orange and a rainbow appears across the hills. After making me trek into the middle of nowhere, Aichi decides to show off. Day 4 The last cookie The chocolate cookies at the venues are a hit. A serious hit. They disappear almost as soon as they arrive, which means that after a few days, spotting a fresh batch creates the sort of urgency usually reserved for breaking news. Late evening at the main media centre, I walk towards the lounge for a coffee and spot one last cookie sitting there. From the opposite direction, I notice a Malaysian journalist heading for the same cookie. He has seen it too. We continue walking, each pretending this is a perfectly normal stroll and not a race for the final chocolate cookie of the evening. We reach it at almost exactly the same time. There is a brief moment of politeness. He offers it to me. I to him. He insists. I insist. Eventually, I take it. India wins. Day 6 100 not out A friend points me to a report in Japan Today, which says the countrys population of people aged 100 or older has crossed one lakh for the first time. The number sounds abstract. Then I look at the volunteers. At subway stations, there are elderly men and women standing beside signs, helping confused tourists find the right platform. At venues, they shepherd athletes through security. At gates, they stand for hours, pointing, explaining, smiling. Some look old enough to be my grandparents. And yet they are here, wearing their volunteer uniforms and doing the most ordinary jobs required to make a giant sporting event work. A few I speak to say they wanted to volunteer at the Tokyo Olympics. The pandemic took that opportunity away. So they are here now. Day 8 Of flavoured KitKat and sake The shooting qualification hall is buzzing with athletes, coaches, officials and the usual post-event shuffle. An Indian shooter finishes his event, opens a matcha-flavoured KitKat and starts eating it. Then comes the story. The previous evening, he accidentally tries the sake-flavoured KitKat. It tasted so bitter. Tasted like desi daaru country-made liquor. He laughs. One finger, apparently, is enough. He tries it once and decides that is quite enough Japanese alcohol for the rest of the trip. Day. I lose track A little Brazil in Toyota Toyota is supposed to be the land of cars. Instead, somewhere between the factories and farms, there is a little piece of Brazil. I know it is Brazil because a football futbol, rather base sits amid open farmland, with low buildings, fields and long stretches of green around it. Then I start noticing the signs. Portuguese. On trains. On hoardings. Around the neighbourhood. Some 60,000-odd Brazilians live in the Aichi prefecture, the highest of any prefecture in Japan. The Brazil-town is not announced with a grand landmark. It is simply there, woven into the landscape. For a few minutes, rural Japan feels slightly Brazilian. Look up A citys fight against screen time I watch the queue inch forward, but almost nobody looks up. Heads are bowed, thumbs flicking, faces lit by the glow of phone screens. A few feet away, people are waiting together, yet each seems to be somewhere else. It feels familiar. We see the same thing all the time in India. But here in Japan, at least one politician has decided to do something about it. Or, more accurately, try. In Toyoake, a city in Aichi, the local government introduced a guideline last year encouraging residents to keep leisure-time smartphone and electronic-device use to about two hours a day. It isnt a ban, there are no penalties, and the city isnt asking people to abandon their phones. The idea is simply to make them look up a little more. The concern, the mayor, Masafumi Koki, tells me, is what gets displaced by those hours sleep, exercise, hobbies and face-to-face conversations. A survey conducted among residents revealed that there is a certain correlation between prolonged smartphone usage and feelings of loneliness, Koki says. A year on, the city is still trying to find out whether the experiment has worked. With 43.2 per cent of participants reporting some behavioural changes or shifts in awareness following the enactment of the ordinance, it is viewed as having been sufficiently effective, Koki says. When the Games leave Usually, the last day of a Games feels like a small bereavement. The venues begin to empty. People who have shared trains, buses, press tribunes and hurried coffees for a fortnight begin saying their goodbyes. There is usually a strange emptiness in the air, the feeling that a little travelling circus is packing itself up and leaving town. This time, I dont feel it. I dont really feel sad that these Games are over. Perhaps because these have been among the strangest Games I have covered. For much of the fortnight, I have had the feeling that Aichi-Nagoya does not really want to host the Asian Games, but is far too polite to say no. So it does what Japan does so well accommodates. Tens of thousands of athletes, officials, volunteers, journalists and support staff arrive, and the city makes room for all of them. But it never quite feels as if the city is curious about them. People dont seem particularly interested in discovering new sports or watching athletes from countries they know little about. The stands remain patchy. The city centre, around which almost everything here seems to revolve, never really feels as though an Asian Games is happening around it. There are no crowds spilling into the streets. No obvious sporting frenzy. No sense that the city has been taken over by the Games. Its strangely fitting then that at the closing ceremony, the biggest cheer comes when Qatars equestrian rider enters the stadium on horseback, takes the Asian Games flag, and then rides out with it. Maybe Nagoyans are simply thrilled by the sight of a horse. Maybe, for a brief moment, the spectacle finally cuts through. Or maybe they are happy that the fortnight is over. On Monday morning, Nagoya gets back to being Nagoya. The trains fill up, and people head to work, as if the Games never happened.

articleTitle: Sanjay Dutt, 67, speaks about bond with daughter Trishala: ‘We had a disconnect’
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Trishala Dutt
description: Sanjay Dutt’s candid admission about his daughter Trishala sheds light on a complicated chapter in their relationship
body_raw: Sanjay Dutt, 67, recently spoke about his 38-year-old daughter, Trishala, who lives in New York, and reflected on their bond. Now she is a big lady. She does a lot of good work there. Its beautiful. I was in New York recently. We spent a lot of time together. We talk about her work, about my work. We had a disconnect in the middle. It happened for many reasons in my case.I was not to have her custody.old story now.I have seen a massive change in her. I am very, very proud of that, Dutt told actor and host Shekhar Suman on his late-night YouTube talk show Shekhar Tonite. Behind the word disconnect lies an experience thousands of families understand intimately, psychotherapist and relationship breakthrough coach Delnna Rrajesh said. Divorce, separation, custody arrangements, legal difficulties, migration and circumstances beyond a childs control can sometimes physically separate a parent and child for years. We often discuss separation through the couples experience the marriage ended, custody was decided, homes changed. But for a child, something entirely different has happened. The relationship ended between two adults the childs family changed without the child ever choosing it. This is where we need greater psychological sensitivity. Custody determines where a child primarily lives and who has particular legal responsibilities it does not, by itself, measure the depth of a parents love or the childs attachment, shared Delnna. DISCLAIMERThis article is based on information from the public domain andor the experts we spoke to. And everyday life matters enormously. Parenthood is not built only through birthdays, holidays and milestone photographs. It is built through school mornings, forgotten water bottles, fevers at midnight, homework, arguments about bedtime, car journeys, teenage moods and conversations that happen unexpectedly over dinner. When a parent and child are separated, these moments disappear. They may still love each other deeply while simultaneously grieving a relationship they are unable to fully live, Delnna told indianexpress.com. Psychology has a useful concept for some experiences of unresolved absence ambiguous loss. Unlike bereavement, where the loss itself is clear, ambiguous loss can involve someone who is still alive and emotionally significant but unavailable in the way they once were or are needed to be. In parent-child separation, the circumstances vary enormously and the concept will not describe every family, but it helps us understand why the grief can be so difficult to articulate. Nobody has died. Yet something precious may still have been lost, said Delnna. Reconciliation often becomes difficult when the parent begins by trying to correct history. That is why the goal shouldnt be to recover the lost years. The healthier task is to build the relationship that is possible now. We cannot retrieve childhood. We cannot attend yesterdays school function, wipe yesterdays tears or recreate yesterdays birthdays. But love does not belong only to the years that were lost. Where there is safety, accountability and willingness, it can also belong to the years that remain. A relationship can have a painful history without being sentenced to a painful future. Sometimes reconciliation is not about getting the past back at all. It is about refusing to let the years already lost take away the years two people may still have, said Delnna. articleTitle: Tom Cruise calls Digger an ‘honour’ as it bombs with $20 mn opening, set to lose $150 mn

description: Alejandro Inarritu's satire Digger has opened at $8 million at the North America box office, which is Tom Cruise's lowest opening weekend in nearly 20 years.
body_raw: Alejandro Inarritus satire Digger, which stars Tom Cruise in the unrecognizable titular role of a greedy oil tycoon, has bombed at the worldwide box office after an underwhelming opening weekend. Irrespective of the trade estimates, Cruise has hailed the film as an honour and a truly unforgettable experience. Digger has earned 20 million at the worldwide box office, 8 million in North America, and Rs 1.55 crore in India. Digger worldwide box office collection Diggers opening weekend of 8 million at the North America box office is far lower than the trade predictions between 12 million and 15 million. After adding 12 million it collected overseas, the total worldwide earnings of the film stand at 20 million after three days. This makes Digger Cruises lowest opening weekend in nearly two decades. As per The Hollywood Reporter, it was 19 years ago that a Tom Cruise film opened lower than 8 million in North America. Robert Redfords 2007 war drama Lions for Lambs, which starred Cruise, Redford, and Meryl Streep, opened at 6.7 million. However, its budget was merely 35 million, almost one-fourth of that of Digger - 125 million. Another 100 million were spent on promotions. As per Guardian, the film is set to lose almost 150 million. For the past 30 years, Cruise has consistently struck gold at the worldwide box office, mostly owing to his popular spy franchise Mission Impossible. Its final instalment which released last year, Christopher McQuarries Mission Impossible - The Final Reckoning, opened at 24.8 million in North America, and 64 million more than three times of Digger in North America. Made on a budget of almost 400 million, it eventually amassed almost 600 million at the worldwide box office. DIGGER is officially in theaters and I am so honored to have had the opportunity to create this film alongside such talented artists. Thank you to the entire cast and crew for your dedication, hard work, and joy. The experience was truly unforgettable and Im so proud of what we created. 13 - Tom Cruise TomCruise October 3, 2026 Despite Cruises superstardom, Digger couldnt even emerge as the box office favourite in North America this weekend. articleTitle: ‘Cristiano Ronaldo should decide how he wants to end his time with national team’, says Portugal coach Jesus
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Ronaldo left Portugal's training camp after being an unused substitute in a win over Norway and learning he would not start against Denmark. (AP Photo)
description: Jorge Jesus said that he had told Cristiano Ronaldo that he needed him, regardless of whether he was playing or not, when he had his first conversation with him after taking charge.
body_raw: Portugal head coach Jorge Jesus has said that it is upto Cristiano Ronaldo to decide if he wants to return to the national team or not. Jesus said that he had told Ronaldo that he needed him, regardless of whether he was playing or not, when he had his first conversation with him after taking charge. If he wants to, hell return to the national team. We can talk before the next call-up, but Cris is the one whos going to decide, Jesus told reporters after Portugals 2-1 Nations League win over Norway on Sunday. Ronaldo left Portugals training camp after being an unused substitute in a win over Norway and learning he would not start against Denmark. He subsequently said on social media that he would explain his reasons for leaving the national team in due course. The incident caused shockwaves around the world of football, with Jesus in particular receiving significant backlash in Portugal for leaving Ronaldo out of the squad. Hes the one who should decide how he wants to end his time with the national team. In my first call-up, I said, I need you, I need you to be close to me, playing or not playing, I need you. And now Im saying the same thing, said Jesus. Portuguese Football Federation President Pedro Proenca also said Ronaldo remained part of the teams plans, describing the episode as a misunderstanding that should be resolved internally. He is in the national team on sporting merit, and that must be unquestionable, Proenca told RTP. We have to pay tribute to Cristiano Ronaldo. In the days after Ronaldo announced his departure, speculation was rife that the 41-year-old may end his illustrious international career. Ronaldo had earlier said that he had briefly considered retiring after the 2026 World Cup. Yes, I thought about it, Ronaldo had told reporters. I always think about my decisions, about the future and also about the present. I am someone who thinks a lot. You have to think. That is why you see me here now. It means I will continue. I think I can give the national team my support, not only through goals but also outside football, he said. My goal is to be able to play, score goals and help the team win matches.

articleTitle: Raju Kher recalls bad phase when brother Anupam Kher refused help: ‘Took him for granted’
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Raju Kher recalls bad phase when brother Anupam Kher refused help
description: Veteran actor Raju Kher, recently recalled a bad phase of his career when he lost everything and expected his brother Anupam Kher to help. However, Anupam was going through challenges in his own life.
body_raw: In the year 2000, both brothers, veteran actors Anupam Kher and Raju Kher were going through a tough career phase. In a new interview, Raju recalled asking Anupam for financial help but later realised how his elder brother was dealing with his own issues, and learnt not to expect anything from him anymore. During a podcast with Siddharth Kannan, Raju Kher revealed shifting to a rented flat after investing his money in a programme on an upcoming new channel. There was a time when I was going through a bad phase. I had sold my house because a new channel was coming, so I had bought a flat elsewhere. A new channel was going to launch and many people were making pilots, agreements were already signed. I also made a programme Life Ke Liye Kuch Bhi Karega, he shared. The veteran actor-director continued, Suddenly, I got to know that the channel has disappeared. I had invested the money that I got from selling the flat in that programme. I thought that I had a first-class life, a 4-BHK house, everything set for the family. And then, the channel disappeared and no one knew what happened.. there was just a lock on their door. During the career setback, Raju Kher reached out to his elder brother, Anupam Kher, for help. He said, I also felt the pressure to pay the rent. I had no one else, I could only talk to my brother, and I thought he will help me. But at that time, he had also stopped working. The reason was that he didnt want to do any of those weird films, he wanted substantial roles. So, I felt that my brother did not help me out. He could have done so, that was my thought at that time. ALSO READ It ended in one day Raju Kher recalls brother Anupam Khers first marriage to Madhumalti However, his perspective towards his brother changed completely after reading a single headline in an article. Then, I was reading a magazine on the toilet. In the interview, Anupam Kher had said, I wish I had my own child. Although, he considers Sikander his own child. But then I never thought about my brother in that light. We took him for granted, thinking he doesnt have any problems because he was doing well financially. We never thought that what was going on in his life. He added, That was the thing that changed the whole concept of my life. Have expectations but dont do it like that. Try to find out what is going in the other persons life as well. I am talking about the year 2000, the year that changed my whole life, my thinking. On that day, I stopped expecting anything from anyone, no matter who it is. When asked about rebuilding his life and career, Raju recalled signing a TV serial after a long phase of no work. When your time is bad, your expenses tend to increase. Some suggested wearing certain rings, doing rituals, prayers, I got those done too. Work had also stopped coming. After a few months, I told my wife that we should trust in God, lets see what happens, and I removed all the rings. The next day, I got a call for work. I got an offer for a TV serial. I instantly agreed and told them to pay whatever they want. Life started again, he concluded. When Anupam revealed taking care of Rajus expenses Earlier this year, during an interaction with Zindagi with Richa Youtube channel, Anupam Kher had revealed that he has been taking care of his brothers finances for years. If every brother remembers what they were like when they were young, there would be no fight. I look at my life like its a film. How can I forget that we grew up together? I must also compliment Kirron Kher, wife, because she never, ever asked me, Why do you do so much for your brother? Thats how problems begin. I would sign cheques for Raju, the household, and other things. I told my manager long ago, Remember one thing in life, never ask me how much money Im giving to my brother.

articleTitle: Employer can’t recover erroneous overpayment from retiree: Karnataka High Court
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Karnataka High Court salary recovery after retirement
description: The Karnataka High Court rules that an excess amount is recoverable only if it was paid on account of any misrepresentation or fraud by the employee.
body_raw: The Karnataka High Court has held that an excess amount paid to an employee while in service cannot be recovered upon retirement if the payment resulted from the employers error. Justice M Nagaprasanna issued this ruling while directing Bangalore Electricity Supply Company Limited Bescom to refund a retired assistant lineman Rs 2,81,887. This amount had been recovered from his pension due to an erroneous increment granted 15 years ago. If the excess amount was not paid on account of any misrepresentation or fraud on the part of the employee, such excess payments of emoluments or allowances are not recoverable, the judge said in his order on September 25. The petitioner, Manjunath N, retired on April 30, 2025. His counsel, Devaraj N, argued that he did not receive the excess pay through fraud or misrepresentation but because of an alleged error by Bescom. Employer admits it cant recover the amount Bescom also admitted that money cannot be recovered from a retired employee unless fraud or misrepresentation on his part is involved. The court referred to a Supreme Court judgment in the case of Jogeswar Sahoo vs District Judge, Cuttack 2025. The judgment held that if the excess amount was not paid due to misrepresentation or fraud by the employee, or if the excess payment resulted from the employer applying a wrong principle for calculating payallowance or based on an interpretation of a ruleorder that was later found to be erroneous, such excess payments of emoluments or allowances are not recoverable. Holding that Manjunath was accused of neither fraud nor misrepresentation regarding the excess amount, the high court directed Bescom to refund it along with interest within eight weeks.

People of Bengal want development and jobs. We have seen that after finishing their education, people leave Bengal for jobs outside because there is a dearth of jobs here. Our leaders Mamata Banerjee and Abhishek Banerjee have already stated that our evaluation of some people was wrong. First, they said no TMC men or women will be taken in the BJP. Then they said they picked good TMC leaders. They should evaluate who are their own party members and who are outsiders, Mitra added. Koel Mallick is the daughter of veteran Bengali film actor Ranjit Mallick and Deepa Mallick. She married film producer Nispal Singh in 2013. She has won several awards for her performances in movies, including a Filmfare Awards Bangla, two Bengali Film Journalists Association awards, and an Anandalok Puraskar.
